# 2026-11-22: Payload mass, and why some properties need a stated band {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T11 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_parameters.py`, `tests/test_bath.py`
:::

**Question.** The [note on ground stiffness](2026-11-22-ground-stiffness.qmd) found that
the body learns the stiffness of the ground from its own thermal motion, at a finite rate.
A payload is the next property of the environment: an unknown mass the leg carries. It
enters the inertia $H$, the kinetic half of the energy metric, where stiffness entered the
potential half. Does the same picture hold?

**Short answer.** Half of it does.

- *One snapshot works the same way, with kinetic energy.* A snapshot of a part's velocity
    carries Fisher information $\frac12\varepsilon^2$ about the log of the mass, where
    $\varepsilon$ is the payload's share of the kinetic energy after a sharp tap on the
    part. Positions in a snapshot say nothing about mass.
- *Over time, the answer depends on how fast a motion is resolved.* Information about the
    mass grows by $(2\varepsilon)^2$ per second for every extra hertz of motion resolved,
    2.25 on the rigid leg, without limit. Damping grows by 1 per hertz. Stiffness does not
    grow: it settles at 833 per second.

The reason is inertia. Above a body's modes, how it moves under any force is set by its
mass, and how hard the thermal force shakes it is set by the damping. So every faster
band of motion gives another look at both. This is not an artifact of white thermal noise:
a thermal bath with finite memory, built here and consistent with fluctuation-dissipation,
gives the same growth. Answers about masses and dampings therefore need a stated band, as
force profiles already have one. In the book's 100 Hz band, the rigid leg's thermal motion
holds 205 per second about the link's mass.

## Setting

The book's rigid leg and SEAs on the clamped bench, with the Langevin body's thermal noise
at $\sigma_T^2=10^{-4}$ J (@sec-langevin). The payload is the link's mass:
$\theta=\log m_l$ around $m_l=3$ kg, with the ground's stiffness and damping held at
$10^6$ N/m and 600 N s/m. On the rigid leg the link carries 75% of the inertia at the joint
($m_lr^2=0.03$ of $H=0.04$ kg m²); the rotor carries the rest. For comparison the note also
treats the ground damping $\theta=\log b_c$ and recalls the ground stiffness.

## Results

::: {#prp-mass-snapshot name="One snapshot of the velocities"}
For a one-coordinate part with velocity $p^\top\dot q$, one snapshot from the Gibbs law
carries Fisher information $\frac12\varepsilon^2$ about $\theta$, with
$$
\varepsilon=\frac{\text{kinetic energy of the payload}}{\text{total kinetic energy}}
\quad\text{after a unit impulse on the part.}
$$
For the velocities of the whole body, $\varepsilon=\operatorname{tr}(H^{-1}\partial_\theta H)$
when $\partial_\theta H$ has rank one. A snapshot of the positions carries no information
about $\theta$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the Gibbs law the velocities are Gaussian with covariance $\sigma_T^2H^{-1}$, and the
positions have covariance $\sigma_T^2K^{-1}$, which does not involve $H$. The rest is the
proof of @prp-snapshot with $H$ in place of $K$: the variance of $p^\top\dot q$ is
$v=\sigma_T^2p^\top H^{-1}p$, and $v'/v=-u^\top(\partial_\theta H)u/(p^\top u)$ with $u=H^{-1}p$,
the velocity after a unit impulse $p$. The kinetic energy is then $\frac12u^\top Hu=\frac12p^\top u$,
and the payload's part of it is $\frac12u^\top(\partial_\theta H)u$. For the whole body,
$\frac12\operatorname{tr}\big((H^{-1}\partial_\theta H)^2\big)=\frac12\varepsilon^2$ when
$\partial_\theta H$ has rank one.
:::

On the rigid leg $\varepsilon=0.75$, the link's share of the inertia, so a snapshot of the
velocity carries 0.281. On the SEA the link is its own coordinate and $H$ is diagonal: the
whole body and the link have $\varepsilon=1$ (0.5), and the rotor's velocity, independent
of the link's in the Gibbs law, carries nothing. The law matches the numbers to $10^{-7}$
(`check_mass_snapshot`).

::: {#prp-inertia-band name="Inertia makes mass information grow with the band"}
Observe the joint angle of the rigid leg over a long window, resolving its motion up to a
band of $B$ hertz. Suppose the thermal force's spectrum does not depend on the mass, and
the leg's response at high frequency is dominated by its inertia. Then, as $B$ grows, the
Fisher information about $\theta=\log m_l$ grows as
$$
\dot I\approx(2\varepsilon)^2\,B\quad\text{per second}.
$$
For the ground damping, whose thermal force has a spectrum proportional to $b_c$, it grows
as $B$. For the ground stiffness it settles.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*Step 1: Whittle's formula.* For a long window, a stationary Gaussian signal with spectrum
$S_\theta(\omega)$ carries Fisher information about $\theta$ at the rate
$\frac1{4\pi}\int(\partial_\theta\log S_\theta)^2d\omega$ per second, the integral running
over the resolved band $|\omega|<2\pi B$.

*Step 2: the spectrum at high frequency.* The angle's spectrum is
$S=|Y(\omega)|^2S_F(\omega)$, with $S_F$ the thermal force's spectrum and $Y$ the leg's
response. At frequencies well above its modes the inertia dominates, $Y\approx-1/(\omega^2H)$,
so $\log S\approx\log S_F-2\log H-4\log\omega$. If $S_F$ does not depend on the mass,
$\partial_\theta\log S\to-2\,\partial_\theta\log H=-2\varepsilon$.

*Step 3: the integral.* The integrand tends to the constant $4\varepsilon^2$, so the integral
over $|\omega|<2\pi B$ grows as $\frac1{4\pi}\cdot4\varepsilon^2\cdot4\pi B=4\varepsilon^2B$.
For the damping, $S_F\propto b_c$ gives $\partial_\theta\log S\to1$ and a growth of $B$. The
stiffness drops out of $Y$ at high frequency, so its integrand decays and the integral
converges.

*What is not proved here.* The error terms of Whittle's formula, and the low-frequency part,
which the numbers give.
:::

On the rigid leg the 0 to 100 Hz band holds 205 per second about the link's mass, and each
further hertz adds 2.25 (@tbl-band). With the whole state sampled at $f_s$, the resolved
band is the Nyquist band $f_s/2$, which is why the information then grows with the
sampling rate. From 2 to 16 kHz it approaches 2.25 per sample with positions and
velocities observed and 1.125 with positions only (`check_resolution`).

### A bath with finite memory does not change this

White thermal noise is an idealization, so a natural suspect is the noise itself. To test
it, every damper is replaced by a Maxwell element, a damper in series with a spring
$\lambda/\tau$, so that the damping relaxes in time $\tau$. With the damping matrix written as
$D=\sum_i\lambda_iu_iu_i^\top$, each element has an internal extension $s_i$, and the thermal
noise acts on $s_i$ rather than on the velocities:
$$
H\ddot q=-Kq-\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i}{\tau}u_is_i,\qquad
ds_i=\big(u_i^\top\dot q-s_i/\tau\big)dt-dW_i/\lambda_i,\quad\E[dW_i^2]=2\sigma_T^2\lambda_i\,dt .
$$
The memory kernel is $De^{-t/\tau}/\tau$ for any choice of elements, so $\tau$ is the only new
parameter, and $\tau\to0$ gives back the Langevin body.

- The Gibbs law, now including the elements' springs, is exactly the stationary law: the
    Lyapunov residual is below $10^{-14}$ (`check_bath`). The bath is consistent with
    fluctuation-dissipation.
- With $\tau=1\,\mu$s the whole body holds 37.743 bits about a 100 Hz force profile,
    against 37.742 with white noise.
- With $\tau=0.1$ ms and 1 ms, the mass information still grows by 2.25 per hertz
    (@tbl-band). The band below 100 Hz changes little at 0.1 ms (204.8) and more at 1 ms
    (312.7), where the bath's memory approaches the ground's relaxation time
    $b_c/k_c=0.6$ ms.

So the growth does not come from white noise. It comes from inertia, as
@prp-inertia-band says, and any bath whose strength does not depend on the mass gives it.

## What this changes

For environmental inputs and for the ground's stiffness, the book's answers are finite
with no added choice: forces come with their own band, and stiffness information settles
by itself. For masses and dampings they are not, and the cause is physical rather than a
modelling shortcut: the faster the motion that is resolved, the more it says about inertia
and about how hard the thermal force shakes the body.

**Proposal for the book.** Give information about masses and dampings for a stated band,
the band of the question, as force profiles already are. The book's 100 Hz band is the
natural default. A body that could follow its own motion at ever higher frequencies would
learn its masses ever better; a lumped model is valid only below its first neglected mode,
which bounds the band anyway.

## Limits of this note

- Checked on the rigid leg, one coordinate. @prp-inertia-band is a proof sketch.
- The bath has one memory time for every damper.
- Fisher information is local, as in the stiffness note.

## Next steps
